doc.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Duo with Bucky and the seven-string
title: Making a living and the rock band on the side
summary: He never decided on a career; duo checks dwarf his rock band pay, and the band played Beatles and other covers.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Did you get to a point on a particular day or time when you said you know I’m going to make my living doing this?

You know I never did. The only thing that I wanted to do I thought was to — I thought somewhere along the line a wrote a lot of pop songs and I thought maybe there was a chance along the way there was going to be some pop music in my future, of performing my own songs and being Billy Joel or James Taylor. And it’s interesting you should ask that question because I never ever realized that I was making a living doing what I was — and I was playing with my dad, and I’d be getting these $600 checks and $1000 checks or whatever, $250, whereas when I was playing dances with my band, I’d be getting $25. And that was like wow. If we had $50 for the gig we were going crazy. And I still had the rock band, because we had fun doing it, and we’d have stretches of down time and I was playing solo gigs and then on the week-end I’d take a rock gig with my band, just playing four chord songs, three chord songs. And my father said, “you’re the only guy playing jazz to support his rock & roll habit.” And he was right. I mean I’d be playing gigs and I’d be giving the money away. Ah we’re having fun here, Doug had the van, give Doug the gas money, I’ll take five bucks and I’ll have another beer. And the drummer, he had to come alone, give him the toll money.
What was your repertoire at the time? CCR and that kind of stuff?

No it was more Beatles. We did all the Beatles covers. So we did “Slow Down,” “Dizzy Miss Lizzie,” “Long Tall Sally,” we did some Allman Brothers songs like “One Way Out,” and we did some Little Feat tunes. It was just wild. We even played a couple of the original songs that were easy to play. And then late at night, this was like a gig we played downtown. We would just fake tunes and it was really horrible. We tried to fake “Live and Let Die,” which okay, with a band, nobody knew what was going on. So we had a lot of fun. And then we’d play BeeGee’s tunes, and play “More than a Woman,” and I’d sing the [scats]. So we were having fun and it was a good release from just everything else. It was nice. But I mean I’d come from gigs in tuxedos with my father, concerts, and go right down. I’d finish, because we’d hit at midnight. I’d finish somewhere at 10:30 and I’d run in and my father’d be shaking his head. “I can’t believe you’re doing this.”
